intro: Abu Dhabi built its grand mosque the way empires used to build cathedrals: slowly, expensively, and without compromise. Eleven years, 3,000 workers, two billion dirhams, and a mountain of white Macedonian marble produced one of the largest mosques on earth, finished in 2007.
page_title: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque - Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Ground was broken in 1996 on a design by Syrian architect Yusef Abdelki, commissioned in the vision of Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the founder of the UAE. More than 3,000 workers from many countries built it over eleven years at a cost of two billion dirhams (US$545 million). Completed on 20 December 2007, the 420-by-290-metre complex holds more than 40,000 worshippers, making it the largest mosque in the UAE and among the largest in the world.
sections.heading: Eleven years of marble

sections.body: The mosque wears 82 domes in seven different sizes, all in white marble with gilded finials and crescents. The main dome is 85 metres high outside and 32.2 metres across, 55 metres high inside, and is counted among the largest domes of its kind. Four minarets of about 104 to 107 metres rise at the corners, deliberately mixing Mamluk, Ottoman and Fatimid vocabularies to speak for the whole Islamic world rather than one tradition.
sections.heading: Eighty-two domes

sections.body: Inside, the numbers keep climbing. The main prayer hall carpet covers 5,627 square metres, weighs 47 tons and holds 2,268,000,000 knots: the largest hand-knotted carpet in the world, made by about 1,200 women to a design by Iranian artist Ali Khaliqi. Seven crystal chandeliers hang in the halls, the largest weighing 12 tonnes with Swarovski crystals and 24-carat gold gilding. Ninety-six columns of the main hall are inlaid with mother of pearl; outside, more than a thousand columns wear 20,000 marble panels inlaid with lapis lazuli, red agate and amethyst.
sections.heading: The carpet and the chandeliers

sections.body: The 17,000-square-metre courtyard is one of the largest marble mosaic artworks anywhere, and the dark-tiled reflective pools double the white colonnades after dark. Lighting designers Speirs + Major gave the mosque a lunar lighting system: the facades glow cold white at full moon and shift gradually bluer as the moon wanes, so the building tracks the Islamic calendar in light.
sections.heading: A calendar in light

sections.body: Furious 7 (2015) brought Hollywood to Abu Dhabi and filmed at the mosque, using it as the backdrop for the Emirates Palace sequences alongside the Etihad Towers jump. The mosque's screen career is young but its photographic one is mature: Slovenian filmmaker Beno Saradzic spent five months shooting it for the time-lapse film The Voyage, assembled from 20,000 frames, which won the time-lapse category at the mosque's own Spaces of Light award. Few buildings have their own photography prize; this one does.

Completed 20 December after eleven years; the world's largest hand-knotted carpet is laid.
